etymologies.etymologyHTML:
The noun is derived from scare (“to frighten, startle, terrify”) +‎ crow (“bird of the genus Corvus”). The word displaced other terms such as bogle (now dialectal, dated), sewel or shewel, and shoy-hoy (perhaps imitative of the cry of crows).

The verb is derived from the noun.

definitions.definition: An effigy, typically made of straw and dressed in old clothes, fixed to a pole in a field to deter birds from eating crops or seeds planted there. [from 1530s]

definitions.definition: (by extension, derogatory) A person regarded as resembling a scarecrow (sense 1) in some way; especially, a tall, thin, awkward person; or a person wearing ragged and tattered clothes.

definitions.definition: (dated) Synonym of crow scarer (“a farmhand employed to scare birds from the fields”)
Anything that appears terrifying but presents no danger; a paper tiger.

definitions.definition: (military, World War II, historical) Military equipment or tactics used to scare and deter rather than cause actual damage.

definitions.definition: To cause (a person, their body, etc.) to look awkward and stiff, like a scarecrow (noun sense 1).

definitions.definition: (archaic) To spoil the appearance of (something, such as the landscape or a view), as scarecrows may be regarded as doing.

quote.citation: 1853 October, “Pike, Salmon, Silurus, Herring, and Company. Esox or Pike.”, in Fraser’s Magazine for Town and Country, volume XLVIII, number CCLXXXVI, London: John W[illiam] Parker and Son, […], →OCLC, footnote *, page 471:
quote.text: Fatigued and hungry as our party were after a long drive through the desolate region of malaria, wild buffaloes, wild birds, and yet wilder specimens of the human race, which here and there scare-crow the broad, sadly picturesque expanse between the last cork-trees near Salerno, and the treeless vicinage of the temple of Neptune, we dared not venture upon fish with green bones,—the only dish served up for our repast;  […]  we all preferred bearing our hunger, and traversing a second time the fiery plain unrefreshed, to breaking our fast upon such suspicious diet;  […]
